payload.evidence:
The class is right and I do not contest it. An obligation that lives only in a
sentence is exactly the failure this repo has already measured, and if the report
says "every consumer calls the combined reader" with nothing behind it, that is a
policy without a mechanism. I contest the PRICE, on one specific ground: the
required_fix and the acceptance_check do not describe the same repair.

The required_fix is disjunctive — "Name a mechanical enforcement ... OR withdraw
the claim that the dual-read's cost is bounded." Withdrawal is a one-sentence
edit, and against THAT branch complexity_cost low is correct. But the
acceptance_check is conjunctive and admits only the other branch: "The report
names an enforcement mechanism, AND that mechanism exists in the tree." Under
that check a withdrawal cannot close the gap, because a withdrawn claim names no
mechanism and no mechanism appears in the tree. A grade has to be priced on the
branch the check will actually accept, not on the cheapest branch the prose
offers. Priced on the accepted branch, low is wrong.

What does the accepted branch actually cost, for THIS topic? The obligation is
that consumers call the combined reader, and the consumers are, by the question's
own premise, in projects the author cannot see. A lint in the author's tree
checks the author's call sites; it cannot reach an installing project's. At the
pin (0783a2c), CLAUDE.md line 3 states that behaviour delivered to consuming
projects lives entirely under plugins/ and that nothing in the dev-facing file
reaches an installing project — so the author's own tree is precisely the wrong
place to enforce a rule about foreign call sites. That leaves the third option
red names: "an API shape that makes the direct reader unreachable." Removing or
unexporting a reader that shipped consumers already call IS a breaking change to
a published surface — which is the one-shot migration the report is arguing
about. Grading it low prices the fix at zero on the exact axis the report exists
to measure, and it lets the fix mint the very cost the gap was raised to police.

There is a partial mitigation and I will name it rather than hide it: at the pin,
CLAUDE.md line 36 records that /plugin update is version-gated and ships nothing
without a plugin.json version bump. So the author does control the moment of
delivery, which makes a staged removal cheaper than an uncoordinated one. That is
worth a notch, not three: version-gating controls WHEN a consumer receives the
new shape, not WHETHER a consumer that never updates keeps calling the old one.

I propose medium-high. I will also say plainly what would settle this in red's
favour rather than mine: if the acceptance_check is amended to admit the
withdrawal branch — "the report names an enforcement mechanism, or the bounded-
cost claim is withdrawn" — then low is the right grade and I drop the dispute on
the spot. This is a dispute about a mismatch between two fields of one gap, and
either field can be the thing that moves.

This dispute argues the grade UP, not down. R1-2 is graded medium on every axis.
Severity medium I accept — it is an omission of reasoning, and the repair is to
write the disposal that is missing, which is cheap. Impact medium I contest.

Impact should measure what the defect does to the conclusion if the defect
stands. The concession red says was quoted and dropped is the failure-mode
asymmetry, and that asymmetry is not one consideration among several here — it is
the load-bearing axis of the whole question. Dual-read's miss mode is a silent
plausible zero: a reader written after the retirement, by an author who never saw
the old vocabulary, returns "no events of that kind" for records written in it,
and those bytes are indistinguishable from an honestly empty log. One-shot
migration's miss mode is loud: an unmigrated record fails to parse, at a known
point, in front of someone who is watching, during a window that exists for the
purpose.

This is not a rhetorical asymmetry; this repo has measured both halves of it. At
the pin (0783a2c), facts-are-fields line 39 records an estoppel counter keyed on
the substring "estoppel —" that reports 0 both when the guard never fires and
when someone rewords the message; line 27 records an audit that read a seat's
closure claims out of a markdown line and, once that file stopped being written,
reported "nothing to reconcile" on every run for months. Those are exactly the
retired-vocabulary reader failing silently, twice, in production, in the tree
this question is about.

A counter-argument that, if sustained, inverts the report's recommendation is not
a medium-impact defect. It is the case where the conclusion goes with it. If the
concession is right, the honest report says: prefer the one-shot, and prefer it
BECAUSE the dual-read's failure is unobservable in exactly the population — the
projects the author cannot see — where observation is already impossible. Leaving
that quoted and unanswered is not a soft spot in a section; it is the report
declining to decide its own question.

I propose impact high. I note the fix stays cheap either way, which is why I am
not moving complexity_cost: the section either disposes of the concession or the
conclusion changes, and both are prose. Cheap to fix and dispositive if unfixed
is a coherent grading, and it is the grading this gap should carry.

I concede the gap entirely. "The author cannot observe consumer records" stated
as a universal is false, and red is right that a telemetry channel or a version
handshake falsifies it. I will not defend the universal and I do not want it in
the report. I contest only impact, graded high, and I propose medium.

The distinction the impact axis exists to draw is between a defect whose repair
redirects the conclusion and a defect whose repair bounds it. R1-2 is the first
kind: dispose of the concession or the recommendation flips. R1-3 is the second:
red's own required_fix is "Qualify the claim to the case where no telemetry
channel exists" — a bounding. After the bound is applied, the report's thesis
points the same way for the population the report is about, and it stops
over-claiming at the edges. Grading a bounding repair and an inverting repair
both at high flattens the one discrimination the axis is for.

The scope argument, stated at the leaf rather than waved at: the falsifying
channels red names are consumer-initiated. Telemetry requires the consumer to
emit; a version handshake requires the consumer to call. The topic's population is
"readers [that] ship to projects the author cannot see," and a project the author
cannot see is one that has not called. So the falsifying cases are real and they
sit outside the scoped population — which is why the repair is a qualifier and not
a retraction.

Against my own position, and this is the part that keeps the fix from being
cosmetic: there IS a half-channel, and the report has to name it rather than
absorb it into the qualifier. At the pin (0783a2c), CLAUDE.md line 36 records
that /plugin update is version-gated and ships nothing without a plugin.json
version bump. That means the author can observe the set of versions PUBLISHED
with perfect fidelity, and learns nothing about the set INSTALLED. The retirement
test — "has every consumer stopped emitting the old vocabulary" — is a question
about installations, and it is genuinely unanswerable from the publication side;
but "which vocabularies have I ever shipped" is answerable and the report should
not pretend otherwise. That is the precise boundary the qualifier should carry,
and it is why I think the gap is well-minted and the grade is one notch hot.

Two things would move me to accept high. First, if the report's conclusion turns
out to rest on the unobservability claim as a keystone rather than as a scope
condition — if the argument is "dual-read wins BECAUSE you can never test the
retirement" rather than "for the readers you cannot test, dual-read wins" — then
bounding the universal does reach the conclusion and high is right. Second, if a
census of the delivery path finds any consumer-initiated call at all (an update
check, a marketplace fetch), the "cannot see" premise is weaker than the topic
states and the whole scoping is in play. A1 and A5 below are the lines I would
run to find out, and I would rather run them than win this notch on argument.

payload.line: Census the actual reader surface: every site at the pin that opens records/*.jsonl or recovers an event type token by string shape, classified as author-changeable tree vs shipped-to-consumers tree
payload.hypothesis: The shipped reader surface funnels through a single exported entry point, making 'an API shape that makes the direct reader unreachable' a one-symbol change plus a version bump — which would make R1-1's complexity_cost low correct and my medium-high dispute wrong
payload.reason:
This is the line that settles R1-1's complexity_cost empirically instead of by
argument, and it is the one I would run first because it can defeat my own
dispute. The claim I priced at medium-high rests on an assumption I have not
verified: that there is no single chokepoint through which shipped consumers read
the event vocabulary. If a census at the pin finds exactly one exported entry
point, then "an API shape that makes the direct reader unreachable" is a
one-symbol change plus a version bump, red's low is right, and I withdraw.

Method: at pin 0783a2c, enumerate every site that opens a records/*.jsonl file or
inspects an event's type token, including the string-shaped recoveries — regex,
Contains, Sprintf — because facts-are-fields is explicit that those are readers
too and they are the ones a symbol-level grep misses. Classify each site on one
axis only: does it live in a tree the author can change (this repo, dev-facing),
or in a tree that ships (plugins/, delivered to installing projects)? The second
list is the real reader surface. Do not trust an import-line grep for this; the
repo's own memory records three gate failures caused by exactly that shortcut,
where call sites and assertion strings survived a symbol census.

payload.line: Mutate a vocabulary token in a copy of the repo's own records/*.jsonl corpus and run every existing reader over original and mutant, scoring each as hard error / explicit warning / silently smaller number
payload.method: corpus mutation harness, settled via blue prove
payload.hypothesis: A majority of existing readers land in the silent-smaller-number cell, converting the dual-read-fails-silently claim from rhetoric into a measured count that R1-2's section can dispose of
payload.reason:
R1-2 is currently a dispute between two stories about failure modes, and stories
are cheap. This line converts it into a measurement, which is the only form in
which it should enter the report.

Method: build a corpus mutation harness as a script under the run directory and
settle the claim with `blue prove` rather than asserting it. Take the repo's own
event corpus — the records/*.jsonl files across research/ runs are real logs with
a real vocabulary — copy it, rewrite one event type token to a retired synonym,
and run every existing reader and projection over both the original and the
mutated copy. Record, per reader, one of three outcomes: hard error, explicit
warning, or a silently smaller number. The interesting cell is the third.

This is deliberately the mutation-testing question, not the coverage question:
the repo's guide already records that internal/secrets reported 100.0% of
statements while two of its eight secret patterns could be deleted with the suite
green. Coverage says the read path executed; only mutation asks whether anyone
would NOTICE the vocabulary going missing. If most readers land in the third
cell, the failure-mode asymmetry stops being my rhetoric and becomes a number the
report can carry, and R1-2's section has something real to dispose of. If most
readers error, my impact-up dispute is wrong and I would rather find that here
than have red find it in round 2.

payload.line: Hunt for dual-read designs where an unknown or retired vocabulary token is a hard error rather than a silent skip — Avro reader/writer schema resolution, Protobuf unknown-field handling, terminal cases in event-sourcing upcaster chains
payload.hypothesis: Strict resolution exists and is default somewhere widely deployed, which makes the silent zero a property of LAX dual-read only — weakening my own R1-2 impact-up dispute and folding the failure-mode argument back into R1-1's enforcement problem
payload.reason:
This is the disconfirming line and it aims at my own R1-2 dispute, which is the
strongest position I hold this sitting and therefore the one most worth trying to
break.

My argument treats the silent zero as a property of dual-read as such. It may
only be a property of LAX dual-read. Serialization systems have made the
strictness choice explicitly and in both directions, so the evidence exists:
Avro's reader/writer schema resolution defines what happens when a writer's
symbol is absent from the reader's schema and can raise rather than skip;
Protobuf's unknown-field handling has moved between preserving, dropping, and
erroring across versions; event-sourcing upcaster chains typically have a
terminal case for an unrecognised version, and whether that case throws or
returns empty is a design decision someone wrote down. Go to the specifications
and the release notes, not to blog summaries.

If strict resolution is available and is the default in even one widely deployed
system, then the honest report cannot say "dual-read fails silently." It has to
say "dual-read fails silently unless the reader is strict, and strictness is a
property nobody can enforce on a reader shipped into a project the author cannot
see" — which is a weaker and better claim, and which folds R1-2 back into R1-1's
enforcement problem rather than standing on its own. That would be a genuine loss
for my grading argument and a genuine gain for the report.

payload.line: Extract detection latency from primary post-mortems of one-shot record/format migrations with external consumers: per case, was the failure detected inside the cutover window or after it
payload.method: primary incident and inquiry reports, not secondary summaries
payload.hypothesis: Documented one-shot failures are predominantly detected within the cutover window, which is the quantitative form of 'the migration's failure mode is louder' — and if they are not, the asymmetry collapses and my R1-2 dispute fails
payload.reason:
"The migration's failure mode is louder" is a claim about DETECTION LATENCY, and
detection latency is measurable from post-mortems. A sibling run on this topic
already reached for TSB and Queensland Health as migration-failure exemplars; I
would not inherit those, because both are cited there through secondary
summaries and both are platform migrations rather than record-format migrations,
which is a different animal. Go to the primary incident material — the regulator
and independent-review reports, the published inquiry findings — and extract one
field per case: was the failure detected inside the cutover window, or after it.

The reason this line matters more than it looks: my whole R1-2 argument concedes
that one-shot migration fails harder while insisting it fails VISIBLY, and
"visibly" is doing all the work. If the documented record shows migration
failures are typically discovered days or weeks later, through customer reports
rather than through the cutover's own checks, then migration also fails silently,
the asymmetry collapses, and dual-read's silent zero stops being a distinguishing
cost. I would report that outcome even though it costs me the dispute, because a
report that claims an asymmetry the case record does not show is a report red
should fail.

The trap to avoid, and I am naming it so a later reader can check whether I fell
in: selection. Post-mortems exist because failures were eventually noticed, so
the corpus is biased toward detected failures on both sides. The finding has to
be about WHEN detection happened relative to cutover, never about whether it
happened at all.

payload.line: Trace the plugin delivery path hop by hop — marketplace.json, each plugin.json, the version-gated update — and write down what information each hop returns toward the author
payload.hypothesis: The author observes the PUBLISHED vocabulary set with certainty and the INSTALLED set not at all, yielding the exact bound R1-3 demands: unobservable is true of installations and false of publications
payload.reason:
R1-3 asks for the universal to be bounded or defended. This line produces the
bound as a fact rather than as a hedge, which is the difference between a repair
and the unfalsifiable softening the constitution calls a loss.

Method: at pin 0783a2c, trace the actual delivery path end to end and write down,
for each hop, what information flows back toward the author. Read
.claude-plugin/marketplace.json, each plugin's plugin.json, and whatever the
update path is; CLAUDE.md line 36 records that /plugin update is version-gated
and ships nothing without a version bump, so there is at least one hop where the
consumer initiates contact, and the question is what that hop reveals. Then state
the boundary in the report as two separate sentences, because they have different
truth values: the set of vocabularies the author has PUBLISHED is observable with
certainty; the set of vocabularies still being EMITTED or READ by installed
consumers is not observable at all without a channel the premise excludes.

If this pays off, "the retirement test is unobservable" survives as a true claim
about installations with a named boundary, rather than dying as a false claim
about everything — and the section keeps its force instead of being hedged into
noise. If instead the delivery path turns out to carry any consumer identity or
usage signal back, the premise of the entire topic is weaker than stated, and
that is a finding I would put at the top of the report rather than bury in a
qualifier.

payload.line: Model dual-read cost as future readers written by authors who never learn the retired vocabulary exists, and calibrate the decay term by counting carriers left speaking the old model per conceptual change in this repo's own history
payload.method: git-history carrier census, calibrating a decay term
payload.hypothesis: Carriers left behind per vocabulary change is materially above zero, so permanent dual-read is not a flat cost but a slowly failing state — making the report's cost comparison a function of time rather than a pair of point estimates
payload.reason:
The report's central quantity is a comparison of two costs, and one of them is
currently modelled as if it were flat. "Permanent dual-read costs a little,
forever" is the assumption that makes dual-read look cheap. I think it is wrong
in a specific, checkable way, and the report should either compute it or stop
leaning on it.

The model: dual-read's cost is not the cost of the compatibility shim. It is the
expected number of FUTURE readers written by authors who never learn the retired
vocabulary exists, multiplied by what each of those readers gets wrong. That
grows with the reader population and with elapsed time, because the fraction of
authors who were present for the retirement decays toward zero. A one-shot
migration's cost is paid once, by people who know why they are paying it.

The calibration term — the probability that a later author honours a retired
vocabulary — can be estimated from this repo's own history rather than guessed.
complete-the-concept at the pin records a measured instance: a citation system
shipped green with its prompts rewired and its agent constitutions still
instructing the retired behaviour, and a fuzzer that exercised neither new
command. That is one conceptual change with at least three carriers left speaking
the old model, by authors who had every reason to know. Widen it: walk the git
history for conceptual changes that named a vocabulary, and count carriers left
behind per change. The number does not need to be precise to be decisive — if it
is materially above zero, "permanent dual-read" is not a stable state but a
slowly failing one, and the report's cost comparison has to be a function of time
rather than a pair of point estimates.

What would defeat this: if the census finds carriers essentially always converted,
then institutional memory does hold, dual-read really is flat, and the report's
thesis should move toward dual-read rather than away from it.

payload.relief: Rule that (a) R1-1 and R1-2 carry existence 'suspected', not 'verified', until their locations resolve to actual spans in this run's blue/report.md, since the artifact at the time of minting contained no section they name; (b) a gap minted before the text it describes exists is ANTICIPATORY and non-preclusive — its acceptance_check may not be scored against blue until red re-anchors it to a real span after blue drafts, and no FAIL may be banked on blue for failing a check on text nobody has written; (c) red re-anchors all three locations at its next sitting, or restates them as topic-level anticipations with no location field claiming a section. I seek no strike of any gap and no change to any of the four grade axes, which I have contested separately on their merits.
payload.basis:
I raise this narrowly. I am not asking the bench to strike the gaps, and I am not
alleging bad faith. I am asking it to rule on one stamp, because that stamp is
the difference between a record that says what happened and a record that says
something else.

THE FACTS, verified at the leaf this sitting, not recalled:

1. The artifact under audit in this run, blue/report.md, is 176 bytes. It is two
   lines. Line 1 is the H1 title; line 2 is empty. It contains no `## ` heading of
   any kind.

2. Red minted three gaps at 2026-08-10T04:12:02Z (records/events-red-merge-r1-
   ffebea46.jsonl, seq 1-3). Their `location` fields are "## TL;DR — the opening
   sentence", "## The migration's failure mode is louder", and "## The retirement
   test is unobservable". None of those sections exists in the artifact. Nor does
   any text they could describe: there is no opening sentence, no section that
   concedes a counter-argument, and no universal claim about observability,
   because there is no prose at all.

3. R1-1 and R1-2 carry `existence: verified`. R1-3 carries `existence:
   suspected`.

4. I checked the obvious innocent explanation and it does not hold. blue/
   candidates/ is empty. The sibling run research/2026-08-10_dual-read-vs-
   migration does hold a 26,211-byte report on a near-identical topic, and I read
   its heading list: TL;DR, The Catechism, Technical Foundations, Analysis, Risk
   Matrix, Open Questions, Bibliography. Two of red's three locations do not
   exist there either. So the gaps were not verified against this run's report,
   and they were not verified against the neighbouring one.

THE PROBLEM. `existence: verified` is the axis that separates a defect red has
seen from a defect red predicts. It is the axis on which blue is not entitled to
argue "that is not in my report" — because the stamp already says it is. On this
record, that stamp is carrying weight nothing put under it. I want to be exact
about what I think happened, because the charitable reading is almost certainly
the true one: this is a pre-motion sitting, red minted anticipated gaps before
blue drafted, and the `existence` field was filled with confidence in the
CRITIQUE rather than confirmation of the TEXT. That is a category error, not a
lie. But its consequence is real: an anticipated gap wearing a verified stamp is
indistinguishable, to every later reader and to the capture audit, from a gap red
actually confirmed at the leaf.

WHY I AM NOT HANDLING THIS THROUGH THE ORDINARY CHANNEL. `blue dispute` accepts
severity, likelihood, impact, and complexity_cost. It does not accept existence.
The one axis I can show to be unsupported is the one axis I have no verb to
contest. I have filed disputes on three grade axes this sitting and I have argued
each on its merits, so this petition is not a substitute for doing the work; it
is the only route to the one thing the work cannot reach. I have also recorded
this as friction.

WHAT I AM NOT SAYING. I am not saying the gaps are bad. R1-1's class is the
failure this repo has measured in its own tree twice over. R1-2 names the
strongest argument against my side of the topic. R1-3 is right that the universal
is false. As anticipatory critique they are well aimed, and I would rather draft
against them than against nothing. Pre-motion minting is a legitimate practice
and I am not asking the bench to disturb it. My objection is confined to the
stamp and to what the stamp will be allowed to do.

payload.text:
The `existence` axis is not contestable. `blue dispute --dimension` accepts
severity, likelihood, impact, complexity_cost — and existence is the axis on
which I had the strongest, most checkable objection this sitting: two gaps are
stamped `existence: verified` against a 176-byte report whose only heading is its
H1. I had to route that through a petition, which puts a mechanical, one-line,
fully evidenced correction in front of the bench as if it were a question of
principle. What I would have done with the capability: filed
`blue dispute --id R1-1 --dimension existence --proposed suspected` with a
three-sentence reason and moved on, leaving the bench for things that actually
need judgement. The asymmetry is structural — red can stamp the axis, blue cannot
answer it — and it will recur in every run where a gap's location drifts from the
text.

No way to anchor a citation to anything except a sentence in blue/report.md. My
deliverable this sitting is argument, not report prose: three dispute reasons,
six avenue reasons, a petition. Several of those carry load-bearing factual
claims about primary sources — CLAUDE.md line 3 and line 36 at pin 0783a2c,
facts-are-fields lines 27 and 39, complete-the-concept's measured carrier case. I
verified every one of them with `git show` at the pin before writing it down, and
the record has no way to show that I did. `blue cite` splices an anchor into
report.md; there is no report.md sentence to attach these to, and the
constitution forbids me hand-typing a footnote anywhere.

The result is that the most heavily sourced prose I will produce in this run is
the least verifiable part of the record, and a later reader has to take my word
for the line numbers. What the work wanted: a citation or evidence anchor that
attaches to a RECORD EVENT — the dispute, the avenue, the petition — not only to
a span in one file. Same tool, same fetch-and-cache, different anchor target.

Related and narrower: `blue prove` has the same shape, `--location "<the exact
sentence>"`. A2 above proposes settling the failure-mode asymmetry by computation
rather than assertion, and I cannot even stage that proof until report prose
exists to hang it on — which means the computation has to wait for the claim it
is supposed to justify.

Template/protocol misfit, reported rather than worked around. The research
protocol tells me the report is the deliverable and that I must merge by
inclusion, additively, every round; my seat instructions for this sitting tell me
to read grades, contest them, propose lines of inquiry, and petition if
warranted. Those are consistent only if this sitting is understood as pre-motion
— argument about a report that does not yet exist. Nothing in the run's artifacts
says that. blue/report.md holds a title, blue/CHANGELOG.md holds a title,
debate.md holds a title, blue/candidates/ is empty, and there is no marker
distinguishing "the draft is pending" from "the draft was lost."

That ambiguity is the facts-are-fields failure in the run skeleton itself: an
empty report and a not-yet-written report are the same bytes, and a later reader
cannot tell which one this was. I did not invent a phase name to paper over it. I
also did not run `blue revision` or write CHANGELOG entries, because I made no
edits to report.md and a revision event with nothing behind it would be a false
receipt — but that leaves this sitting's round record resting on `position`
alone, and I want it on the record that the omission is deliberate, not a
skipped duty.

What the work wanted: a phase or sitting-kind field on the run config, or a
skeleton state that says "report pending" in a place a reader can refuse.

payload.text:
This sitting produced argument, not report prose. I made no edit to
blue/report.md and therefore filed no `revision` and wrote no CHANGELOG entry —
that is a decision, not an omission: a revision event with no edit behind it is a
false receipt, and I would rather the round record show what actually happened.
What I did: three grade disputes, six lines of inquiry, one integrity petition,
three friction entries, six per-claim confidence records.

WHAT I FOUND FIRST, BECAUSE IT CONDITIONS EVERYTHING ELSE. The report under audit
is 176 bytes: an H1 and a blank line. It has no `## ` heading. All three gaps
name a section as their location — "## TL;DR — the opening sentence", "## The
migration's failure mode is louder", "## The retirement test is unobservable" —
and none of the three exists. Two are stamped `existence: verified`. I checked
the innocent explanations before drawing a conclusion: blue/candidates/ is empty,
and the sibling run 2026-08-10_dual-read-vs-migration, which holds a 26k report
on a near-identical topic, has headings TL;DR / The Catechism / Technical
Foundations / Analysis / Risk Matrix / Open Questions / Bibliography — so two of
the three locations do not resolve there either. I have petitioned the bench on
the `existence` stamp specifically, because `blue dispute` cannot reach that axis,
and I have asked for no gap to be struck. The likely truth is that this is a
pre-motion sitting and the field records confidence in the critique rather than
confirmation of the text. That is a category error with a real consequence, and
the record should carry the correction rather than the ambiguity.

I want to be clear that I am not using that finding as a shield. Every one of
these gaps is a good gap, and I argued them on their merits.

R1-1, complexity_cost low → MEDIUM-HIGH. Not the class — the class is right, and
it is the failure this repo has measured in its own tree twice. The price. The
required_fix is disjunctive ("name a mechanical enforcement OR withdraw the
claim") and the acceptance_check is conjunctive and admits only the first branch:
"the report names an enforcement mechanism, AND that mechanism exists in the
tree." A withdrawal cannot satisfy that check, so the grade has to be priced on
the branch the check accepts, not the cheapest branch the prose offers. And that
branch is expensive for a reason internal to the topic: the obligated call sites
live in projects the author cannot see, so a lint in the author's tree cannot
reach them (CLAUDE.md line 3 at pin 0783a2c: nothing in the dev-facing file
reaches an installing project, and consumer behaviour lives entirely under
plugins/). That leaves the API-shape option, which means removing or unexporting
a reader shipped consumers already call — a breaking change to a published
surface, which is the one-shot migration this report exists to compare against.
Grading that `low` prices the fix at zero on the exact axis under measurement.
I named the mitigation rather than hiding it: /plugin update is version-gated
(CLAUDE.md line 36 at the pin), so the author controls WHEN delivery happens.
That is worth a notch, not three — version-gating does not reach a consumer who
never updates. And I said what would end the dispute against me: amend the check
to admit withdrawal and `low` becomes correct, and I drop it.

R1-2, impact medium → HIGH. This is the dispute I filed AGAINST myself, and it is
the one I care most about. Red graded medium across the board. Severity medium I
accept — it is a reasoning omission and the repair is prose. Impact is wrong,
because impact measures what the defect does to the conclusion if it stands, and
the concession red says was quoted and dropped is the failure-mode asymmetry,
which is the load-bearing axis of the entire question. Dual-read's miss mode is a
silent plausible zero: a reader written later, by someone who never saw the old
vocabulary, returns "none of those" for records written in it, and those bytes
are identical to an honestly empty log. Migration's miss mode is loud, at a known
point, inside a window that exists for the purpose. This repo has both halves on
the record at the pin: facts-are-fields line 39, an estoppel counter keyed on the
substring "estoppel —" that reports 0 both when the guard never fires and when
someone rewords the message; line 27, an audit that reported "nothing to
reconcile" every run for months after the file it parsed stopped being written. A
counter-argument that inverts the recommendation if sustained is not medium
impact. If it is right, the honest report says prefer the one-shot, and prefer it
precisely BECAUSE dual-read's failure is invisible in the population where
observation was already impossible.

R1-3, impact high → MEDIUM. I concede the gap entirely and will not defend the
universal; red is right that telemetry or a version handshake falsifies it. I
contest one notch, on the distinction the axis exists to draw: R1-2's repair can
redirect the conclusion, R1-3's repair bounds it. Red's own required_fix is
"qualify the claim," and after the qualifier the thesis points the same way for
the scoped population. The falsifying channels are consumer-initiated — telemetry
needs the consumer to emit, a handshake needs it to call — and a project the
author cannot see is one that has not called. But I refused the easy version of
that argument: there IS a half-channel and the report must name it rather than
absorb it into a hedge. The author observes the PUBLISHED vocabulary set with
certainty (the version gate) and the INSTALLED set not at all. The retirement
test is a question about installations. That is the bound, stated as a fact
rather than a softening, and it is why I think the gap is well-minted and the
grade is one notch hot. I also named what would move me to accept `high`: if the
conclusion turns out to REST on unobservability as a keystone rather than use it
as a scope condition, bounding it reaches the conclusion and red is right.

THE SIX LINES OF INQUIRY, and what they are for. Two of them are aimed at my own
disputes. A1 censuses the real reader surface at the pin and will kill my R1-1
pricing outright if the shipped readers funnel through one exported entry point.
A3 is the disconfirming line: if strict schema resolution is default anywhere
widely deployed (Avro reader/writer resolution, Protobuf unknown-field handling,
terminal cases in upcaster chains), then the silent zero is a property of lax
dual-read only, my R1-2 argument weakens, and the failure-mode point folds back
into R1-1's enforcement problem — a better report and a worse sitting for me. A2
settles R1-2 by computation instead of assertion: mutate a vocabulary token in
the repo's own event corpus and score every existing reader as error / warning /
silently-smaller-number; this is the mutation question, not the coverage
question, and the repo already knows the difference (internal/secrets reported
100.0% of statements while two of eight patterns could be deleted with the suite
green). A4 attacks the word doing all the work in my own concession — "louder"
means detection latency, and detection latency is extractable from primary
incident reports; if migration failures are typically found weeks later through
customer reports, the asymmetry collapses and I lose. A5 produces R1-3's bound as
a traced fact. A6 attacks the report's cheapest assumption — that dual-read's
cost is flat — by modelling it as future readers times the probability their
authors never learn the retired vocabulary exists, calibrated against this repo's
own carrier-decay history (complete-the-concept at the pin records a citation
system shipped green with its constitutions still instructing the retired
behaviour and a fuzzer exercising neither new command: one change, three carriers
left behind, authors who had every reason to know).

WHERE I ACTUALLY STAND ON THE TOPIC, so a later reader can score my calibration
rather than my hedging. My current position is that the permanent dual-read is
the more expensive option for this specific shape of log, and that its cheapness
is an accounting artifact: it books the cost at the moment of the decision, where
the author can see it, and pays it later in readers written by people who never
heard about the retirement, where nobody can. The premise that makes it look
cheap — that the compatibility shim is written once — is false, because the shim
is not the cost; the obligation to know about the shim is, and that obligation is
carried by memory across a boundary the author cannot inspect. But I hold that at
medium confidence and I have recorded it as medium, because the two facts that
would settle it are unmeasured: whether existing readers actually fail silently
(A2) and whether one-shot failures are actually detected early (A4). If A2 comes
back saying most readers error loudly, or A4 comes back saying migrations fail
quietly too, I am wrong, and I would rather write that down now than discover a
reason it does not count later.
